The execution the solution itself traces relaxes each edge exactly once: R(n) = |E_n| = n(n-1)/2 = Theta(n^2). Crucially this is not an artifact of one implementation: ORACLE #2 exhaustively searches every legal execution of generalized Dijkstra-with-re-insertion (the algorithm must extract an active vertex of minimum tentative distance, but the adversary resolves every priority-queue tie arbitrarily), and the MAXIMUM Relax count over all of them is the exact cubic R_max(n) = (n^3 - 3n^2 + 8n - 6)/6 - verified against the exhaustive search at every n = 2..18, third finite difference constantly 1. Highest-index-first tie-breaking attains that maximum exactly.

So R_max(n) = Theta(n^3) = o(2^n): the claimed lower bound fails at EVERY n >= 2, and the ratio R_max(n)/(2^n - 1) decays geometrically (0.4667 at n=4, 0.2471 at n=8, 0.0564 at n=12, 0.0032 at n=18 - a factor of 315 short). Since ORACLE #2 is a true upper bound over all Dijkstra implementations on G_n, no choice of priority queue, tie-breaking, or re-insertion policy can rescue the bound; the family is simply not exponential.

Mechanism of the failure: w(v_i,v_j) = -2^i depends only on the TAIL index i, so the improvement a vertex offers all of its successors is fixed once that vertex's own label is fixed. Labels descend along the single chain v_0 -> v_1 -> ... -> v_j to the true optimum -(2^j - 1) (confirmed by ORACLE #1, exhaustive enumeration of every v_0 -> v_j path with exact ints, agreeing with the implementation for all n = 1..12), and vertices settle in index order. There is no binary-counter cascade and hence no exponential number of strict decreases. The solution's induction is independently invalid on its own terms: at lines 0029-0038 it sums R(n-j) over the suffix subgraphs {v_j,...,v_{n-1}} for j = 1..n-1, but those suffix subgraphs are nested and share edges, so the same relaxations are counted many times over; the recurrence R(n) >= (n-1) + sum_j R(n-j) has no valid derivation from the algorithm's behaviour. Line 0023's base case is also arithmetically wrong (it asserts 0 = 2^1 - 1 = 1).
faithfulness_notes: The solution's construction is fully explicit (lines 0005-0008: vertex set, edge set, weight rule) and was implemented verbatim; the graph was verified to be a DAG (all edges strictly forward) with all weights negative, matching the problem's constraints. The solution never states its Dijkstra variant precisely, which is the one implementability gap - but it is not load-bearing against the solution, because we resolved it in the direction most favourable to the claim: (a) the primary implementation is lazy-priority-queue Dijkstra that re-enqueues a vertex on every strict distance decrease and re-processes it when popped with a current key, which is exactly the re-processing behaviour the solution's own trace at lines 0013-0017 describes and the only variant under which an exponential Relax count is even conceivable (textbook extract-once Dijkstra relaxes each edge at most once by construction); (b) we additionally ran textbook extract-once Dijkstra; and (c) ORACLE #2 quantifies over EVERY legal execution of the re-insertion variant, so the refutation holds for any reading of the variant, any priority queue, and any tie-breaking rule. The Relax counting convention also favours the solution: we count one Relax per outgoing edge examined, not just per successful decrease. Source is v_0 per line 0013. All arithmetic is exact Python ints (unreached distances are represented as None rather than a float infinity, so no float ever participates in a comparison); the measurement is a pure operation counter, never wall clock; the run is fully deterministic with no sampling. Nothing in the solution was repaired or invented.
